pr.body:
**What is this feature?**

Writes to annotations are sometimes rejected on MySQL due to a recurring deadlock with the annotation cleanup job.
Details here: https://github.com/grafana/grafana/issues/64979

**Why do we need this feature?**

The deadlock seems to be a result of the subquery, under normal circumstances a plain insert and delete should not lock, and there are no extended transactions at play.

This PR splits the subquery into a separate SQL statement. These statements do not share a transaction, and therefore allow locks to flush in between.

Unfortunately we could not reduce this to a single DELETE statement, due to the batching - DELETE LIMIT is not supported on all databases without needing to reintroduce the subquery. The IDs loaded into memory are of bounded size due to the batch size configuration.

**Which issue(s) does this PR fix?**:

https://github.com/grafana/grafana/issues/64979

**Special notes for your reviewer:**

Please check that:
- [x] It works as expected from a user's perspective.
- [x] If this is a pre-GA feature, it is behind a feature toggle.
- [x] The docs are updated, and if this is a [notable improvement](https://grafana.com/docs/writers-toolkit/writing-guide/contribute-release-notes/#how-to-determine-if-content-belongs-in-a-whats-new-document), it's added to our [What's New](https://grafana.com/docs/writers-toolkit/writing-guide/contribute-release-notes/) doc.

raw_findings.body: Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so building the IN-list is O(n^2) in bytes: for ~32k IDs this copies hundreds of megabytes per batch and noticeably slows every cleanup batch.
raw_findings.failure_mode: CPU and allocation cost of the cleanup job grows quadratically with the configured batch size.
raw_findings.impact: Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so building the IN-list is O(n^2) in bytes: for ~32k IDs this copies hundreds of megabytes per batch and noticeably slows every cleanup batch.
raw_findings.root_cause: The new inline-values code path accumulates the ID list by re-formatting the entire string on each element.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Build the list with a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.FormatInt` into a slice joined by `strings.Join`) instead of repeated `fmt.Sprintf` accumulation.
raw_findings.title: Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for large SQLite batches
raw_findings.trigger: SQLite deployment with `annotations.cleanupjob_batchsize` above 999 (the new test uses 32767), so each batch inlines tens of thousands of IDs.

raw_findings.body: The generated DELETE carries one bind parameter per ID and is rejected by the server, so annotation cleanup fails with an error on every cycle; previously the single-statement subquery used no parameters and had no such limit.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Cleanup job errors out for large configured batch sizes on parameter-limited drivers.
raw_findings.impact: The generated DELETE carries one bind parameter per ID and is rejected by the server, so annotation cleanup fails with an error on every cycle; previously the single-statement subquery used no parameters and had no such limit.
raw_findings.root_cause: The new delete-by-IDs implementation binds one placeholder per ID and only special-cases the SQLite limit.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Chunk `ids` into fixed-size groups (e.g. 999 or a per-dialect maximum) inside `deleteByIDs` and issue one DELETE per chunk, instead of assuming any configured batch size fits into one parameterized statement.
raw_findings.title: Parameterized DELETE can exceed driver placeholder limits on non-SQLite databases
raw_findings.trigger: Postgres (or MySQL) deployment with `annotations.cleanupjob_batchsize` configured above the server/driver bind-parameter limit (65535 for the Postgres wire protocol).

validated_findings.impact: All cleanup jobs (temp files, snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history) now run 10x more often, multiplying background DB load; because each run is bounded by a 9-minute timeout, a long-running cleanup is immediately re-triggered on the next tick, keeping the DB permanently under cleanup load.
validated_findings.root_cause: A debugging-only tick interval change was committed together with the annotation deadlock fix.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Revert the interval to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)`; this change is unrelated to splitting the annotation cleanup queries and looks like leftover local debugging.
validated_findings.title: Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
validated_findings.trigger: Any Grafana instance running the background CleanUpService after this patch is deployed.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Patch line 77 shows `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` replacing `time.Minute * 10`. This 10x frequency increase is introduced by the patch and affects all cleanup jobs. The 9-minute timeout combined with 1-minute ticks creates the described overlap risk.

validated_findings.impact: Successful operations are reported as errors, polluting logs and triggering error-rate alerting; the `err` field is always nil here because the error was already returned above, and the full ID slice bloats each log line.

validated_findings.suggested_fix: Remove these two diagnostic log lines (also the companion `r.log.Error("cleaned annotations by time", ...)` on the next lines) or downgrade them to `r.log.Debug` without dumping the whole `ids` slice and without the always-nil `err`.

Using Error level for successful operations with nil err is a debug leftover.

validated_findings.body: Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so building the IN-list is O(n^2) in bytes: for ~32k IDs this copies hundreds of megabytes per batch and noticeably slows every cleanup batch.
validated_findings.failure_mode: CPU and allocation cost of the cleanup job grows quadratically with the configured batch size.
validated_findings.impact: Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so building the IN-list is O(n^2) in bytes: for ~32k IDs this copies hundreds of megabytes per batch and noticeably slows every cleanup batch.
validated_findings.root_cause: The new inline-values code path accumulates the ID list by re-formatting the entire string on each element.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Build the list with a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.FormatInt` into a slice joined by `strings.Join`) instead of repeated `fmt.Sprintf` accumulation.
validated_findings.title: Quadratic string concatenation when inlining IDs for large SQLite batches
validated_findings.trigger: SQLite deployment with `annotations.cleanupjob_batchsize` above 999 (the new test uses 32767), so each batch inlines tens of thousands of IDs.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Line 611 shows `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` in a loop, which is O(n²) string concatenation. For batch sizes above 999 on SQLite (line 608 condition), this creates quadratic allocation cost. The trigger is realistic given configurable batch size up to 32767 in tests.

validated_findings.body: The generated DELETE carries one bind parameter per ID and is rejected by the server, so annotation cleanup fails with an error on every cycle; previously the single-statement subquery used no parameters and had no such limit.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Cleanup job errors out for large configured batch sizes on parameter-limited drivers.
validated_findings.impact: The generated DELETE carries one bind parameter per ID and is rejected by the server, so annotation cleanup fails with an error on every cycle; previously the single-statement subquery used no parameters and had no such limit.
validated_findings.root_cause: The new delete-by-IDs implementation binds one placeholder per ID and only special-cases the SQLite limit.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Chunk `ids` into fixed-size groups (e.g. 999 or a per-dialect maximum) inside `deleteByIDs` and issue one DELETE per chunk, instead of assuming any configured batch size fits into one parameterized statement.
validated_findings.title: Parameterized DELETE can exceed driver placeholder limits on non-SQLite databases
validated_findings.trigger: Postgres (or MySQL) deployment with `annotations.cleanupjob_batchsize` configured above the server/driver bind-parameter limit (65535 for the Postgres wire protocol).
validated_findings.verifier_reason: The claim about exceeding placeholder limits on Postgres/MySQL is speculative. The default batch size is 100 (line 710 in setting.go), and Postgres limit is 65535. The patch only special-cases SQLite. No evidence that realistic configurations would hit this limit.

validated_findings.body: An error value is bound to a variable named `y` and returned unchecked-looking, which hides that the second result is an error and makes the batch callbacks harder to review and maintain; it also violates the surrounding code's `affected, err :=` convention.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Reduced readability and higher chance of mishandling the returned error in future edits.
validated_findings.impact: An error value is bound to a variable named `y` and returned unchecked-looking, which hides that the second result is an error and makes the batch callbacks harder to review and maintain; it also violates the surrounding code's `affected, err :=` convention.
validated_findings.root_cause: Placeholder variable names from prototyping were kept in the new batch-work closures.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Rename to `affected, err := r.deleteByIDs(...)` (and likewise in the max-count and orphaned-tag closures) so the error result is obvious.
validated_findings.title: Non-descriptive `x, y` names for the affected-count and error results
validated_findings.trigger: Reading or modifying the three new cleanup closures, which all use the same `x, y := r.deleteByIDs(...)` pattern.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: This is a style/readability issue about `x, y` variable names. The category is correctly marked as 'style'. While the naming is poor, it's not a bug - the error is still returned correctly via `return x, y`. Dropping as stylistic.

validated_findings.body: The subtest no longer runs cleanup a second time over already-cleaned data — it merely seeds 9 fresh annotations — so the idempotency behaviour the name advertises is untested while the name suggests it is covered.
validated_findings.evidence: name:                          "running the max count delete again should not remove any annotations",
validated_findings.failure_mode: Test suite silently loses idempotency coverage while the case name implies it still exists.
validated_findings.impact: The subtest no longer runs cleanup a second time over already-cleaned data — it merely seeds 9 fresh annotations — so the idempotency behaviour the name advertises is untested while the name suggests it is covered.
validated_findings.root_cause: Converting the previously state-dependent, sequential test cases into independent self-seeding cases dropped the second cleanup invocation but kept the old case name.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Either invoke `cleaner.Run` twice within this subtest and assert zero affected rows on the second call, or rename the case to reflect what it now verifies (e.g. "max count delete removes nothing when count is already at the limit").
validated_findings.title: Test case name claims a repeat run that the rewritten test no longer performs
validated_findings.trigger: Running TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp after this patch, where each subtest now seeds its own data and truncates it in `t.Cleanup`.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: The test case at line 83 now seeds 9 annotations with `createAnnotationsNum: 9` and expects `affectedAnnotations: 0`. This tests that when count equals MaxCount (3*3=9), nothing is deleted. The name is misleading but the test still validates the boundary condition, not idempotency per se. This is a minor test naming issue, not a test gap.

validated_findings.body: Because the truncation hook is not yet registered, the seeded annotation/annotation_tag rows survive into the following subtests on the shared `fakeSQL` database, turning one failure into a cascade of unrelated assertion failures that hide the original cause.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Cross-subtest state leakage on failure makes the integration test results non-deterministic and hard to diagnose.
validated_findings.impact: Because the truncation hook is not yet registered, the seeded annotation/annotation_tag rows survive into the following subtests on the shared `fakeSQL` database, turning one failure into a cascade of unrelated assertion failures that hide the original cause.
validated_findings.root_cause: The cleanup hook was moved into the subtest but placed after the data-seeding and verification calls that can abort the subtest.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Register the `t.Cleanup` deleting `annotation` and `annotation_tag` as the first statement of the subtest, before `createTestAnnotations` and the count assertions.
validated_findings.title: Per-subtest data cleanup is registered after seeding and assertions
validated_findings.trigger: A failure inside `createTestAnnotations` or the two `assertAnnotationCount`/`assertAnnotationTagCount` calls that precede this registration (they call `require`, which aborts the subtest).
validated_findings.verifier_reason: The t.Cleanup registration at line 120 comes after createTestAnnotations (line 116) and assertions (lines 117-118). However, t.Cleanup functions are deferred and run regardless of test failure. The cleanup will still execute even if earlier lines fail. The ordering concern is not a real bug.

validated_findings.body: The case inserts 40003 annotations plus 80006 annotation_tag rows and then deletes 40000 of them on every backend, adding minutes to each integration test job, even though the scenario it names (SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER) only exercises the SQLite inline-values branch of `deleteByIDs`.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Integration suite wall-clock time grows substantially for coverage that a much smaller dataset would provide.
validated_findings.impact: The case inserts 40003 annotations plus 80006 annotation_tag rows and then deletes 40000 of them on every backend, adding minutes to each integration test job, even though the scenario it names (SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER) only exercises the SQLite inline-values branch of `deleteByIDs`.
validated_findings.root_cause: The regression case sizes its dataset far beyond what is needed to trigger the >999-parameter code path and is not scoped to the dialect it targets.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Reduce the row count to just above the batch size (or gate this case on `db.IsTestDbSQLite()`) so the SQLite parameter-limit branch is still exercised without seeding ~120k rows on every backend.
validated_findings.title: New 40003-row test case inflates runtime of every integration DB run
validated_findings.trigger: Running TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp against any backend (SQLite, MySQL, Postgres) in CI.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: The 40003-row test case is intentionally large to test the SQLite parameter limit workaround. While it adds runtime, this is a deliberate test design choice to ensure the >999 parameter path works. The test is gated by integration test skip. This is a test design tradeoff, not a defect.
